unit.title: Teaching programming and algorithms at university

video.title: Assessing programming at scale: Autograders, tests and academic integrity
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.

chapters.label: Integrity in the age of AI

scenes.narration: Four hundred students, one assignment, two teaching assistants. Last term the autograder passed code that only worked on the visible tests. How do you grade fairly at this scale?
Today: how to design autograded programming assignments that measure understanding, how to find and teach bugs, and how to protect integrity when AI can write the code.
An autograder runs each submission against a test suite and reports a score. It is fast and consistent. But it only measures what the tests check, so test design is assessment design.
Give students visible tests for fast feedback. Keep hidden tests for edge cases such as empty input, duplicates and very large values. Code that hard-codes the visible answers then fails.
This median passes the visible test. It always picks the middle element. A hidden test finds it, and the feedback message should name the case without giving the fix.
Tests check correctness, not design or understanding. Combine an autograded part with a short code-reading task and a written explanation. Add a brief oral check for a random sample.

AI assistants can now solve most introductory assignments. Detection tools are unreliable, so design for it instead. State clearly what help is allowed, weight in-person and explained work more, and ask students to modify or extend code live.
Quick check! The median code passes the visible test. Which hidden test exposes its bug?
A list with an even number of items, such as one, two, three, four. The correct median is two and a half, but the code returns three.
In the app, open the bugs lab. Run each of the six programs, fix it, and write the one-line hint you would give a student, without the fix.
Your turn. Which assessment change best shows that a student understands code they submitted?
Asking them to modify it live and explain the change. Remember: hidden tests catch shortcuts, feedback names the case, and understanding needs more than a passing score.

scenes.narration: Try it in your next lecture: show a submission that passes the visible tests and ask pairs to write one hidden test that breaks it. Collect the best tests and add them to next term's suite.

checkpoints.prompt: The median code passes the visible test. Which hidden test exposes its bug?
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: odd and sorted lists work; even lengths need the average of two middles.

checkpoints.prompt: Which change best shows a student understands their submitted code?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: live modification shows understanding directly.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: detectors are unreliable and tests only check output.
